newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Unemployment a key threat to Albania - World Bank.
newsitem.headline: Unemployment a key threat to Albania - World Bank.

text.p: Spiralling unemployment poses one of the most serious threats to Albania in the wake of the country's recent crisis, the World Bank's resident representative in Albania, Carlos Elbirt, said on Tuesday.

The violence that swept Albania towards anarchy in March after popular pyramid investment schemes collapsed brought revenue collection to a virtual halt, exacerbated an already worrying budget deficit and hammered the lek as inflation rose.
Elbirt said the collapse of the funds and ensuing chaos hit the service sector hard, which posed a grave danger to unemployment.

"The service sector suffered a lot because of the events, the (dusk-to-dawn) curfew that was imposed, the departure of foreign investors and the lack of security," Elbirt told Reuters in an interview.
"The bad news is that this sector is very labour intensive."
Before the crisis, the number of registered unemployed in Albania was 12 percent although the actual figure was believed much higher in the Balkan nation of 3.4 million people.
"With the slowdown in economic activity and foreign investment, unemployment could really surge," Elbirt said.
"This is one of the main challenges now facing the country...and our main concern.
"A result of increasing unemployment could be to expand the poverty in Albania and we may see an increase in criminality."
Albania's economy was already in trouble before the funds fiasco which wiped out thousands of people's life savings.

Market reforms implemented after the 1990 fall of communism had turned Albania into Europe's fastest-growing economy with Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth of about 10 percent a year between 1993 and 1995 albeit from a low base.
Albania remains Europe's poorest state, needing to catch up after 46 years of isolation under hardline Stalinist rule.
From late 1995, the budget deficit started to expand. Spending by the Democratic Party government rose ahead of a general election in May 1996 and local elections in October.
GDP growth in 1996 slipped to 5.5 percent, to $2.3 billion.
Some economists also partly attributed the GDP slowdown to the end of a U.N. oil embargo on Serbia and Montenegro.

An Economist Intelligence Unit report said during the Yugoslav conflict a highly lucrative fuel trade developed between Albania and Montenegro. The Albania Centre for Economic Research estimated illegal petrol exports to Serbia accounted for 10-15 percent of GDP between 1993 and 1995.
The budget deficit in 1996 rose to about 11 percent of GDP from seven percent in 1995, and in 1997 is seen at 15 percent.

An interim all-party government appointed in Albania on March 9 after the Democratic Party government resigned has forecast GDP will fall to around seven percent in 1997. Agriculture accounts for about half of GDP and should not be affected.
Elbirt said urgent action was needed in Albania to keep the economy in check, stabilising prices and a currency which has depreciated by a third against the dollar this year.
He said the first priority was to restore security.
Unofficial estimates say up to one million weapons were looted from state arsenals in the unrest and armed gangs now roam the country with poorly equipped police powerless.
Elbirt said the second step was to recompose the budget focusing on the collection side.
In the violence in February and March, many government buildings were destroyed, major ports closed, and businesses halted, bringing tax and customs collection to a standstill.
"Finally the government needs to rapidly create the conditions for expansion of economic activities, to relaunch the development agenda here," Elbirt said.
